paras: The peonage and disappearance of Cornelius Alexander was a 1920 case in Pike County, Georgia, in which a Black laborer held to work off a debt went missing and federal investigators exhumed a body identified as his near Holtinsville. Members of the white Connell family were indicted for peonage, and the New York Age presented the case as proof that slavery survived in Georgia.

According to an Atlanta Constitution account relayed by the Age, Alexander worked in 1918 for Matt Bottom, a white farmer of Concord, to pay a $40 debt. Frank Huff then assumed a $175 debt Bottom claimed, and in December 1918 passed Alexander to Robert Connell, who credited him $20 a month against it. Alexander ran away from Connell's plantation in August 1919.

He went to Atlanta with a badly bruised head and asked the district attorney for protection against Beecher Connell, who he said had beaten him for disobeying Willard Connell, Beecher's brother. Advised not to return, he took a garage job in Douglasville.

In February 1920 Willard Connell and the Pike County sheriff arrested him there, and he was held in the Zebulon jail. Philip Moore, a Connell tenant, secured his release and said he paid Robert Connell $22.50 a month for Alexander's labor, which went unpaid. Some weeks before August 1920 he disappeared; a decomposed body identified as his was later exhumed.

Federal authorities took up the case, and the Connells were indicted on a charge of peonage. The Age wrote that the investigation "may lead to the discovery of the murderers," but no cause of death, inquest, arrest or trial outcome appears in the coverage.

The New York Age carried the case on August 7, 1920, in an editorial headed "Slavery in Georgia". It declared that "Negro slavery may still be found in the state of Georgia" and noted that the $40 debt had only grown. Calling the creditors "robber landlords," it said the case was "not solitary" and urged federal action.
The Constitution's original story and any other white-press report do not appear in the coverage examined.

reader.title: Peonage and disappearance of Cornelius Alexander
bases: The editorial describes Alexander held for years at forced labor against a growing debt, passed from employer to employer, jailed and hired out, with the Connells indicted for peonage; his disappearance and the exhumed body are reported as part of that case (A1).
The only report is one New York Age editorial (A1, with an OCR duplicate A2) that relays an Atlanta Constitution story; no white-press original or other account was found.

accounts.label: Atlanta Constitution, as relayed by the New York Age
accounts.gist: Alexander was passed along a chain of white employers on a mounting debt, beaten, arrested and jailed after he ran away, hired out without wages, and then disappeared; federal agents exhumed a body identified as his and the Connells were indicted for peonage.

accounts.label: Alexander's own complaint (1919)
accounts.gist: Alexander told the district attorney in Atlanta that Beecher Connell beat him for refusing an order of Willard Connell.

accounts.label: Philip Moore's statement
accounts.gist: Moore said he paid Robert Connell $22.50 a month for Alexander's services while Alexander received no wages.

framing.detail: Under the headline 'Slavery in Georgia', the Age wrote that 'Negro slavery may still be found' in Georgia, called the landlords 'robber landlords', said the case 'is not solitary', and urged the Department of Justice to take up such cases.

record_check.dossier: Holtinsville in the clean text; 'Hollinsville' appears only in the garbled duplicate. It is where the body was exhumed, not necessarily where Alexander disappeared (stated only as Pike County).
Disappearance 'some weeks ago' before the August 7, 1920 editorial (itself relaying a 'recent' Constitution story); approximate only. The peonage ran from 1918 to 1920.
1 presumed dead: body identified as Alexander's exhumed; cause of death and killers not reported; murder only suggested
Killers unnamed; the Connells (Robert, Beecher, Willard) indicted for peonage, Beecher Connell accused by Alexander of the earlier beating
Also arrest and jailing for debt at Zebulon with the Pike County sheriff, and hiring out without wages

record_check.record: held in peonage on the Connell plantation ... disappeared
record_check.dossier: When he disappeared he had been released from the Zebulon jail to Philip Moore, a tenant on the Connell plantation, who paid Robert Connell for his labor

info: Alexander disappeared 'some weeks' before the editorial of August 7, 1920; no exact date is given
Disappeared in Pike County; body exhumed near Holtinsville in the same county

Beecher Connell, a white plantation owner, was named by Alexander as having beaten him a year earlier; Robert Connell and his sons held Alexander's labor; the persons who may have killed him are not named
1 presumed: a badly decomposed body identified as Alexander's was exhumed; no cause of death is reported, and the editorial only says the inquiry 'may lead to the discovery of the murderers'

sources.note: Editorial 'Slavery in Georgia' relaying an Atlanta Constitution account: debt chain, beating, arrest, forced labor, disappearance, exhumed body, Connells indicted for peonage.
quotes: in this year of Our Lord One Thousand Nineteen Hundred and Twenty, Negro slavery may still be found in the state of Georgia.
Federal investigators of the Department of Justice exhumed a body in a badly decomposed condition near Holtinsville in the same county, which was identified as that of the missing man.
Moore stated that he paid Robert Connell, father of the Connell brothers, $22.50 a month for Alexander's services, while the colored man received no wages at all.
the Connells have been indicted, charged with peonage, the investigation may lead to the discovery of the murderers of the man who so mysteriously disappeared.
Ignorant Negroes contract a small debt with these robber landlords, and are held through fear to work it out.

sources.note: Garbled OCR duplicate of the same editorial on the same page, with headline 'SLAVERY IN GEORGIA'; place printed 'Hollinsville'; no additional facts.
